oneLineAnswer: A prescription immunosuppressant given after an organ transplant to stop the body rejecting a donated kidney, heart or liver.
whatItIs: Mycophenolate mofetil is a prescription medicine sold as capsules, tablets, an oral liquid and an injection. Regulators call it an antimetabolite immunosuppressant. An immunosuppressant is a medicine that lowers the activity of the immune system. An antimetabolite disrupts substances that cells use to grow and multiply. In the United States the approved use is organ transplant patients, and it is not a supplement.
whatItDoes: Your immune system normally attacks anything it sees as foreign, and a donated organ looks foreign.
Mycophenolate mofetil damps that response so a transplanted kidney, heart or liver is less likely to be rejected.
The label says it is given together with other immunosuppressant medicines, not by itself.
The label describes it as an antimetabolite, meaning it interferes with building blocks that multiplying immune cells rely on.
Rejection is the immune system attacking the new organ.
howPeopleUseIt: In the label's trials, patients took it by mouth or by vein after a kidney, heart or liver transplant.
The label says it should be managed by a doctor with experience in immunosuppressive therapy.
Trial records list studies of it in lupus nephritis, an immune-related kidney disease.
Other trial records compare different tablet versions in healthy volunteers.
The label notes the oral capsules and tablets are not interchangeable with a delayed-release tablet form sold as mycophenolic acid.

commonSideEffects: Trials reported diarrhea, low white blood cell counts, infection and vomiting in 20 percent or more of patients.
Some of those infections were opportunistic, meaning they take advantage of a weakened immune system.
The same trials also recorded low red blood cells, low platelets, stomach upset, headache and dizziness.
seriousSigns: A boxed warning means the strongest safety warning a United States label can carry.
The boxed warning names three serious risks: harm to a fetus, lymphoma and other cancers, and serious infections.
Skin cancers are the cancers the label flags most often.
Blood problems listed include shortages of white cells, platelets and red cells.
Gut problems listed include bleeding, ulcers and a perforation, which is a hole forming in the bowel wall.
The label also lists a rare inflammatory reaction that works against expectations.
It warns that the medicine may affect your ability to drive or run machines.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone allergic to mycophenolate mofetil or to mycophenolic acid should not use it.
The label says to avoid it in pregnancy when a safer treatment is available.
People with a rare inherited enzyme problem called HGPRT deficiency should avoid it.
People taking it are told not to donate blood during treatment or for 6 weeks afterward.
Sperm donation is not advised during treatment or for 90 days after it ends.

interactions: Antacids that contain magnesium or aluminum lower how much of the medicine your body absorbs.
Stomach acid reducers called proton pump inhibitors, such as lansoprazole and pantoprazole, can do the same.
Cholestyramine, rifampin and several antibiotic families can also lower drug levels in the body.
Telmisartan lowers those levels, while the antifungal isavuconazole raises them.
The label says the medicine may reduce how well oral contraceptives work, so an added barrier method is recommended.
Drugs cleared through the kidneys, such as acyclovir and ganciclovir, may build up in the body.
Live vaccines are to be avoided during treatment.
pregnancyAndChildren: Mycophenolate mofetil is not safe in pregnancy. The boxed warning links it to pregnancy loss in the first trimester and to birth defects. Registry data cited in the label put first trimester loss at 45 to 49 percent. Birth defects were reported in 23 to 27 percent of live births in those registries. Reported problems include cleft lip and palate, ear and eye differences, and heart, kidney and limb defects. The label says to avoid the drug in pregnancy when a safer option exists. Men taking it are advised to use effective birth control during treatment and for 90 days after. There is no data on how much passes into human milk. The label covers children from 3 months old for kidney, heart and liver transplants.
whatWeDoNotKnow: There is no human data on whether mycophenolate enters breast milk or changes milk production.
The label's main transplant trials ran about 12 months, so effects beyond that are less certain.
It is unclear how much of the cancer and infection risk comes from this drug itself.
Studies of the drug outside transplant have been small, unfinished or stopped early.
The label gives no way to predict who will develop the rare gut or liver complications.

summary: This record covers what mycophenolate mofetil is, why it is used after organ transplant, the side effects and serious risks the FDA label records, its known interactions, and pregnancy and children information, drawn from the FDA drug label and public clinical trial registry data.
